newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing survivors testify about blast.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing survivors testify about blast.

text.p: Survivors of the Oklahoma City bombing, the first witnesses in the trial of Timothy McVeigh, on Friday vividly recreated the morning of the blast, recalling desperate searches for loved ones lost in the rubble.
A television cameraman, one of the initial witnesses in the first day of testimony, described a tap on his shoulder as he filmed the devastation at the Alfred P. Murrah building on April 19, 1995.
"There was a young lady who said to me, 'Sir, my baby is in the day care. Can you help me?'" he testified in the crowded Denver courtroom. He said he gave her a cellphone and a warm coat.
Weeks later, he learned that her baby was 6-month-old Lee Gottshall, who died in the bombing. Nineteen children were among the 168 people killed.
Susan Hunt, a survivor who worked at the Department of Housing and Urban Development, testified how she helped her injured co-workers after the blast.
One woman said, "'I can't see. Do I have an eye?'" she testified. "I didn't answer her because she didn't."
Hunt also said the parents of babies in the day-care centre were scrambling to get into the collapsed building, and "we were holding them back. We didn't want anyone else getting hurt."

The day's court proceedings began with the sounds of a massive roar as jurors listened to a dramatic recording of the blast, captured on a tape of a hearing of the Oklahoma Water Resources Board across the street from the federal building.
After about two minutes of voices, the tape is interrupted by a huge roar, crashes, rumblings and the frightened shout of "Let's get out of here."
Victims' family members in the courtroom tensed visibly at the start of the harrowing tape and reached for one another tearfully as the deadly explosion was heard.
The prosecution claims McVeigh, motivated by anti- government hatred and extremist politics, blew up the federal building in hopes of provoking a "second American Revolution."
Defence attorney Stephen Jones has tried to undermine the government's case by suggesting the possibility of an uncaptured accomplice, confused eyewitnesses and FBI mishandling of the evidence.

McVeigh, 29, wearing an open-necked white shirt and khaki trousers, kept his head down and took notes. The tall, thin Gulf War veteran has pleaded not guilty to murder and conspiracy charges and could face the death penalty if convicted.

He showed no emotion as the HUD worker recalled her co- worker Lee Sells chatting with a friend just before the explosion. Asked by a prosecutor if she ever heard Sells' voice again, Hunt replied, "No, I did not."
Roy Sells, seated in the courtroom, bowed his head and began to cry at the mention of his late wife. Thirty-five of HUD's 124 employees in the building perished.

Former Marine Corps recruiter Michael Norfleet testified that the bomb "filleted open" his right eye, leaving him partly blind and destroying his dreams of being a pilot. He said he had followed a trail of blood as he fled the Murrah building.
Norfleet recalled parking that morning in front of a Ryder truck outside the building and thinking it was odd for the truck to be there. That truck was used to carry the bomb.
He also testified that he did not see McVeigh at the scene.

During the afternoon session, U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch announced that Jones, McVeigh's lead attorney, had been called away temporarily on a personal emergency and other members of the defence team would handle the case.
